A LL's gone! ſtill thou'rt a Gentleman, that's all; but a poore one, that's nothing: What Milke brings thy Meadowes forth now? where are thy goodly Vp-lands and thy Downe-lands, all ſunck into that little pitte Lecherie? why ſhould a Gallant pay but two ſhillings for his Ordnary that nouriſhes him, and twenty times two for his Brothell that conſumes him? but where's Long-acre? in my Vncles conſcience, which is 3. yeares voyage about; he that ſetts out vpon his conſcience, nere finds the way home againe, he is either ſwallowed in the quick-ſands of Law-quillits, or ſplits vpo ̄ the Piles of a Praemunire; yet theſe old Foxe-braind—and oxe-browde Vncles, haue ſtill defences for their Auarice, and Apologies for their practiſes, and will thus greete our follyes. Hee that doth his youth expoſe, To Brothell, drinke, and danger, Let him that is his neereſt Kinne, Cheate him before a ſtranger. And that's his Vncle, 'tis a principle in Vſury; I dare not viſit the Cittie, there I ſhould bee too ſoone viſited, by that horri ble plague my Debts, and by that meanes I looſe a Virgins loue, her portion and her Vertues, well, how ſhould a man liue now, that ha's no liuing; hum? why are there not a million of men in the world, that onely ſoiourne vpon their braine, and make their wittes their Mercers; and am I but one amongſt that Million and cannot thriue vpon't; any Trick out of the compaſſe of Lawe now, would come happily to me.
My loue. I begin to applaud thee, our States beeing both deſpe rate, they' are ſoone reſolute, but how for horſes? Arme your wittes then ſpeedily, there ſhall want no thing in mee, eyther in behauiour, diſcourſe or faſhion, that ſhall diſcredit your entended purpoſe. I will ſo art-fully diſguiſe my wants, And ſet ſo good a courage on my ſtate, That I will be beleeued. Tis right the world, for in theſe dayes an olde mans loue to his kindred, is like his kindneſſe to his wife, 'tis alwayes done before hee comes at it. Is he ſo ſir? I thinke ſo? Maiſter Wit-good? where are you? Nor land, nor liuing ſay you, pray take heede you do not wrong the Gentleman? Is my loue ſo deceau'd, before you all I do renounce him, on my knees I vow He nere ſhall marry mee,— The world is ſo deceitfull? Pray ſir. Vp ſtaires! troth I am weary Maiſter Wit-good Nay I commend your care, tis donne well of you? aſſe what haue I forgot. I ſlipt my wedding Ring off when I waſht, and left it at my lodging, prethee run, I ſhall be ſad without it, ſo, hee's gon!—boye? Husband and Gentlemen, heare me but a word. Let him in peaceably, you know we're ſure, from any act of his. Was it not cauſe too much? Send to enquire his ſtate, moſt part of it, Lay two yeares morgag'd in his Vncles hands: • ut y'aue beene euer full of golden • peech, If wordes were lands, your Nephew would bee rich. I do proteſt before theſe Gentlemen, I will be as cleere then, as I am now. Hum? faith ſir twould like me better here, here you were married, here let all rites be ended. Alaſſe his creditors ſo mercileſſe, my ſtate beeing yet vncertaine, I deeme it not vnconſcionable to furder him. Curſt be my raſh and vnaduiſed words, Ile ſet my foote vpon my tongue, And tread my inconſiderate grant to duſt. No ſir, ide haue it done ſome Nobler way Of your ſide; ide haue you come off with honor, Let baſeneſſe keepe with them: why haue you not the meanes ſir, the occaſions offerd you. No more,—why do your worſt for that, I defie you. Call vp thy wits for thou haſt beene deuoted to follies a long time. Deſpiſe me, publiſh me I am your wife, What ſhame can I haue now but youle haue part, If in diſgrace you ſhare, I ſought not you: You purſued me, nay forc'ſt me, Had I friends would follow it, Leſſe then your action has beene prou'd a rape. Nor did I euer boaſt of lands vnto you, Money or goods: I tooke a playner courſe: And told you true ide nothing, If error were committed twas by you. thanke your owne folly, nor has my ſinne beene ſo odious but worſe has bin for giuen, nor am I ſo deformd but I may challing the vtmoſt power of any old mans loue, ſhee that taſts not ſin before, twenty to one but ſheele taſt it after: moſt of you ould men are content to mary yong Virgins and take that which followes, where marrying one of vs, you both ſaue a ſinner, and are quit from a cuckold for euer, "And more in breife let this your beſt thoughts winne, "She that knowes ſinne, knowes beſt how to hate ſinne.
My lothing; haſt thou beene the ſecret conſumption of my purſe? and now comſt to vndo my laſt meanes, my wits? wilt leaue no vertue in me and yet thou nere the better? hence Cur tizan, round webd Tarantula. That dryeſt the Roſes in the cheekes of youth. For giue I do thee wrong, To make thee ſinne, and then to chid thee fort. Stay beſt inuention,—ſtay. I prethee, make me not mad at my owne weapon, ſtay, (a thing few women can do I know that, and therefore they had need weare ſtayes;) be not contrary, doſt loue me? Fate has ſo caſt it that all my meanes I muſt deriue from thee. Spoke like an honeſt drab ifaith, it may proue ſom-thing what Trick is not an Embrion at firſt, vntil a perfect ſhape come ouer it. So, ſo, ſo, thou ſhall preſently take the name and forme vpon thee of a rich country widdow foure hundred a yeare va liant, in Woods, in Bullocks, in Barnes and in Rye-ſtacks, weele to London ▪ and to my couetous Vncle. Mine Hoſt? Dooſt thou ioy in my aduancement? Comes my proſperitie deſiredly to thee? I ha brought her from her friends, turnde backe the Horſes by a ſlight, not ſo much as one amongſt her ſixe men, goodly large Yeomanly fellowes, will ſhee truſt with this her purpoſe: by this light all vnmand; regardleſſe of her ſtate, neg lectfull of vaine-glorious ceremonie, all for my loue; oh 'tis a fine little voluble toung mine Hoſte, that wins a widdow. How the deuill came he not by it, if you put in the deuill once riches come with a vengeance, has beene a Trampler of the Law ſir, and the deuill has a care of his footemen, the Roague has ſpied me now, hee nibled me finely once too; a poxe ſearch you, oh maiſter Dampit, the very Loynes of thee; crie you mer cie maiſter Gulfe, you walke ſo lowe I promiſe you I ſawe you not ſir? And nyer hell by a foote and a halfe then the reſt of his fellowes, but my old Harry. Twas a merry world when thou cam'ſt to towne with ten ſhillings in thy purſe. And when to the ſellar agen? Did'ſt thou ſo old Harry ? Tramplers of time. Ah thou'rt a mad old Harrie ? kinde Maiſter Gulfe, I am bould to renew my acquaintance. Vncle I thanke you. Will you but heare what I can ſay in my iuſt excuſe ſir. You that know my danger ith Citty ſir ſo well, how great my debts are, and how extreame my Creditors could not out of your pure iudgment ſir, haue wiſht vs hether. My credit? nay my countenance, puſh, nay I know vncle you would haue wrought it ſo by your wit you would haue made her beleeue in time the whole houſe had beene mine — La you there; wel, let e'm al prate what they will ther's nothing like the bringing of a widdow to ones Vncles houſe. There they may be bold. Troth I thinke I can vncle. Pray command one of your men hether Vncle. I ha ſent ſir? Heauen forbid Vncle? Troth I confeſſe it Vncle, I was too blame there, but in deed my intent was to haue clapt it vp ſuddainely, and ſo haue broke forth like a ioye to my friends, and a wonder to the world, beſide there's a trifle of a forty pound matter towarde the ſetting of mee forth, my friends ſhould nere haue knowne on't, I meant to make ſhift for that my ſelfe ▪ To me alaſſe, what do you meane Vncle? Y'aue no reaſon for that Vncle. Nay and you ſay ſo Vncle, here's my hand, I will not doote — Good Aunt— And the wit in the pommell, good Maiſter Sam fredome I returne the ſalute. Vncle? My Vncle was deſirous to ſee you widdow, and I prae ſum'd to enuite you. Sir — Alaſſe ſir, I know not how ſhee would take it: Why alaſſe, my Creditors? could you finde no other time to vndo mee but now, rather your malice appeares in this then the iuſtneſſe of the debt. I pray ſpeake lowe ſir, what do you meane? What can bee kept ſo cloſſe but you creditors here on't, wel, tis a lamentable ſtate, that our cheifeſt afflicters ſhould firſt heare of our fortunes, why this is no good courſe yfaith ſirs, if euer you haue hope to bee ſatiſfied, why doe you ſeeke to con found the meanes that ſhould worke it, there's neither piety, no nor policy in that, ſhine fauorably now, why I may rize and ſpred agen, to your great comforts. Remoue me now, and I conſume for euer. How can it thriue which from the Sun you ſeuer. Oh then ſhow patience, I ſhall haue ynough to ſatiſfie you all. For looke you, I am but newly ſure yet to the widdow, & what a Rend might this diſcredit make: within theſe 3. daies will I binde you lands for your ſecurities. I know you haue beene kinde, how euer now either by wrong report, or falſe incitement your gentleneſſe is iniurde, in ſuch a ſtate as this a man cannot want foes. If on the ſuddaine he begin to rize, No man that liues can count his enimyes. You had ſome intelligence I warrant yee, from an ill-willer. I, why there it was, I knew twas ſo, but ſince you are ſo wel reſolude of my faith toward you, let me be ſo much fauor'd of you, I beſeech you all — As to lie ſtill a while, and bury my debts in ſilence, till I be fully poſſeſt of the widdow, for the truth is, I may tell you as my friends — I am to raiſe a little money in the Citty, toward the ſet ting forth of my ſelfe, for mine owne credit, and your comfort, now if my former debts ſhould be diuulg'd, all hope of my pro ceedings were quite extinguiſht! You doe ſo rauiſh mee with kindneſſe, that I'me con ſtrainde, to play the maide and take it? Fah— Beleeue it firmely. Not I beleeue it. I know e'm. Say you ſo, why here's my hand then no man liuing ſhal do't but thy ſelfe. I faith ſhalt thou? Would twere all in Plate, You haue the better tearme by my faith Excellent, Wench, make vp thy owne fortunes now, do thy ſelfe a good turne once in thy Dayes, hees rich in money, moueables, and lands, —marry him, he's an old doting foole, and thats worth all, marry him, twould bee a great comfort to me to ſee thee do well ifaith, —marry him, twould eaſe my conſcience well to ſee thee well deſtowd, I haue a care of thee ifaith. I reach at farder happines; firſt I am ſure it can be no harme to thee, and there may happen goodnes to me by it, proſecute it well, lets ſend vp for out witts, now we require their beſt and moſt pregnant Aſſiſtance! Heauen knowes hee neuer meant it? Oh for more ſcope, I could laugh eternally, Giue you ioye Miſtres Hoord, I promiſe your fortune was good forſooth, y'aue fell vpon wealth ynough, and there's young Gentlemen enow can helpe you to the reſt; now it requires our wits: carry thy ſelfe but heedfully now, and wee are both— Cuds me, remoue thy ſelfe a while, ile ſerue for him? The ſame to you kinde Vncle. Oh no queſtion of that ſir? The ſooner the better Vncle, oh ſhee's mightily fol lowed, — Mightily? here comes one old Gentleman, and heele make her a ioynture of three hundred a yeare forſooth, another welthy ſuiter wil eſtate his ſonne in his life time, and make him weigh downe the widdow, here a Merchants ſonne wil poſſeſſe, her with no leſſe then three goodly Lordſhips at once, which were all pawnes to his Father. Oh my pretious Vncle. Reſt your ſelfe here a while widdowe, wee'le haue a cup of Muſcadine in this little Roome. But do you heare ſirrah. What is there prouided for dinner Againſt you are ready to drinck to mee, widdow, ile bee preſent to pledge you. I muſt requeſt you ſir, to ſhow extraordinary care, my Vn cle comes with Gentlemen his friends, and tis vpon a making? Who he widdow? Withall my heart ifayth, ile bring you to her? How now, boy, drawer. Went the Gentlewoman vp that was here? Out ſir? Hoord, death and darkeneſſe, Hoord. How now, what newes, where's the widdow? More madnes yet. Poore ſoule he knew not on't. Thats all my comfort Vncle, ha, ha, ha. Now may euents fall luckily, and well, He that nere ſtriues, ſayes wit ſhall nere excell. To be borne from me by that lecher Hoord. I beſeech you Gentlemen. To gladſome, to be true. Nothing afflicts me ſo much, But that it is your Aduerſary, Vncle, And meerely plotted in deſpite of you. I know it ſir? I were worſe then a beaſt elſe ifayth. Heaven forbid elſe. Alaſſe a thing quickly done Vncle. Pray let me vnderſtand you rightly, Vncle, You giue it me but in truſt. That is, you truſt me with it. But if euer I truſt you with it agen, would I might bee truſt vp for my labour. Hee has no conſcience, faith would laugh at them, they laugh at one another? Who then can be ſo cruell, troth, not I, I rather pitty now, then ought enuie, I do conceiue ſuch ioye in mine owne happineſſe, I haue no ley ſure yet, to laugh at their follies. Thou ſoule of my eſtate I kiſſe thee, I miſſe lifes Comfort when I miſſe thee. Oh neuer will we part agen, Ʋ ntill I leaue the Sight of men, We'le nere truſt conſcience of our kin, Since Cooſenage brings that title in. My laſt ioy was ſo great it tooke away the ſence of all future afflictions, what a day is here orecaſt? how ſoone a black tempeſt riſes? You do well my maiſters, to tiranize ouer miſery to af flect the affl • cted, tis a cuſtome you haue here amongſt you, I would wiſh you neuer leaue it and I hope youle do as I bid you Pray ſirs ▪ youle giue me Breath. Will you but here me ſpeake? Giue me but reaſonable time, and I proteſt Ile make you ample Satiſfaction. Tis true, beaſts know no reaſonable time, Alaſſe what good will my carcaſſe do you? I perceiue I muſt craue a litle more Ayde from my wits, do but make ſhift for me this once, and Ile forſweare euer to trouble you in the like faſhion hereafter, Ile haue better em ployment for you, and I liue. Youle giue me leaue my maiſters to make Tryall of my friends and raiſe all meanes I can. Oh art thou come! No by my faith canſt thou. I am in hell here and the Deuills will not let me Come to thee. I when your miſcheifes ſpent. Wel, what then? you wil pay none of my debts I am ſure. Shall I remember thee of an other promiſe far ſtronger then the firſt. Harke in your ear.—will hee come of thinkſt thou, and pay my Debts roundly. Excellent. A my troth I could not, for my creditors cruelties ex tend to the preſent. Y'are impudent, ile call vp witneſſes. Would you ſo, I thanke you for that ſir, I cannot blame you ifayth. Are not words promiſes, and are not promiſes debts ſir. My Vncle wi • l nere endure me, when he ſhall heare I ſet my hand to a releaſe: Say you ſo ſir? Proceede then, I conſent. What a pretious fortune haſt thou ſlipt here like a beaſt as thou art? well Maiſter Hoord, giue me the pen, I ſee Tis vaine to quarrell with our deſtiny. Troth, and it were pit • y of my heart now, if I ſhould beare you any grudge yfaith. I hope to bring it to paſſe my ſelfe ſir? Ile try theſe fellowes now, —a word ſir, what will you carry me to that widdow now? Farewell and be hangd, you ſhort-pig-hayrde Ram-head ed raskalls, he that beleeues in you, ſhall nere be ſau'd I warrant him, by this new league, I ſhall haue ſome acceſſe vnto my loue — A words ynough. Let the Vſurer cram him, in intereſt that excell, There's pits enow to dam him, before he comes to hell. In Holborne, ſome: in Fleete-ſtreet ſome, Ʋ Ʋ here ere he come, there's ſome there's ſome. Nay vncle, let me preuayle with you ſo much, Ifaith go, now he has enuited you, Why la, I thought where I ſhould find you preſently; Vncle, a my troth, tis nothing ſo. No by my troth is he not Vncle. Will you haue the truth out, he is married to a whore ifaith. Vncle, let me periſh in your fauour if you find it not ſo and that tis I that haue married the honeſt woman. And ſee'te you ſhall, or Ile nere ſee you agen. Negatur, ſequela maioris, Vncle, hee that knowes a wo man to be a queane, muſt needes be a knaue, I deny that. And are not you and I ſworne perpetuall friends before wittneſſe ſir, and were both drunck vpon't. Nay now you wrong her ſir ▪ if I were ſhee ide haue the lawe on you for that, I durſt depoſe for her, ſhee nere had com mon vſe, nor common thought. Alaſſe ſir, I was prick tin conſcience to ſee her well beſtowd ▪ and where could I beſtowe her beter then vpon your pittifull worſhip: excepting but my ſelfe, I dare ſweare ſhees a Virgin, and now by marrying your Neece I haue baniſht my ſelfe for euer from her, ſhe's mine Aunt now by my faith, and theres no Medling with mine Aunt you know, a ſinne againſt my Nuncle. I muſt confeſſe my follyes, Ile downe to And Here for euer I diſclaime, The cauſe of youths vndooing. Game: Cheifly dice, thoſe true outlanders, That ſhake out Beggars, Theeues and Panders, Soule waſting Surfets, ſinfull Riotts, Queanes Euills, Doctors diets. Pothecaries Drugs, Surgeons Gliſters, Stabbing of armes for a common Miſtris, Riband fauours ▪ Ribauld Speeches, Deere perfumde Iacketts, pennyleſſe breeches, Dutch Flapdragons, healths in Vrine, Drabs that keepe a man to ſure in: I do defie you all. Lend me each honeſt hand, for here I riſe, A reclaymde man loathing the generall vice.
I haue beene true vnto your pleaſure, and all your lands thrice rackt, was neuer worth the Iewell which I prodigally gaue you, my virginity; Lands morgag'd may returne and more eſteemde, But honeſty once pawnd, is nere redeemd. I know I am your loathing now, farewell. I that haue beene the ſecret conſumption of your purſe ſhall I ſtay now to vndo your laſt meanes, your witts? hence Currizan away. From me! be happy then, What lies within the power of my performance, Shall be commanded of thee. Come I muſt helpe you where abouts left you, Ile proceed. Tho you beget, tis I muſt helpe to breed, Speake what iſt, Ide faine conceaue it. Rich Newes! There's ſome in chaines and Iewells, I am ſo haunted with ſhuters Maiſter Wit-good, I know not which to diſpatch firſt. Among the number, one Maiſter Hoord an Antient Gentleman. It may well hold ſo, for he rayles on you, Speakes ſhamefully of him. I firſt denyed him, but ſo cunningly, It rather promiſde him aſſured hopes, Then any loſſe of labour. I expect him euery hower, with Gentlemen, With whome he labours to make good his words, To approue you Riotous, your ſtate conſumde, your Vncle,— Thankes ſweete maiſter Wit-good. Step in, I thinke I heare e'm. Y are wellcome Maiſter Hoord. I cannot tell, How my affections may diſpoſe of me, But ſurely if they find him ſo deſartleſſe, Theyle haue that reaſon to with-draw them-ſelues. And therefore Gentlemen I doe entreat you, As you are faire in Reputation, And in appearing forme ſo ſhine in truth; I am a widdow and alaſſe you knowe, Soone ouerthowen, tis a very ſmall thing, That we with-ſtand, our weakenes is ſo great, Be partiall vnto neither, but deliuer, Without affection your opinion, It ſuffizes? Alaſſe, how ſoone are wee poore ſoules beguild! Alaſſe, you loue not widdowes but for wealth, I promiſe you I ha nothing ſir, Now I muſt hope the beſt, But Maiſter Hoord, one thing I muſ • remember you of before theſe gentlemen your friends, how ſhall I ſuddainly auoyde the loathed Solleciting of that periurd Wit-good, and his Tedious—diſſembling Vncle, who this very uery day hath appointed a meeting for the ſame purpoſe too, where had not truth come forth I had beene vndon, vtterly vndon. In that it pleaſeth you, it likes me well. Farwell ſir.— Come hether ſirrah, learne ſecretly if one Maiſter Hoord an antient Gentleman be about houſe? Commend me to him. Oh you come well: away, to boate, be gon. I had I but ſeene any ſuch thing perform'd why twould haue tyed my affection and contaynd me in my firſt deſires, doe you thinke ifayth, that I could twine ſuch a dry, oake as this, had promiſe in your Nephew tooke effect: When I ſhall heare this done, I ſhall ſoone yeeld, to reaſonable tearmes. I, with all my heart. Thats all I waite for. Faith ſpoke to eaſe his minde,— You know now, little to any purpoſe. He would do mountaines now. I did ſir? Some fooliſh words I muſt confeſſe did paſſe, Which, now letigiouſly he faſtens on me. Too ſtrong I feare, would I were well free'd of him. Hee is now caught by his creditors, the ſlaue's needie, his debts petty, hee'le rather binde himſelfe, to all inconuenien ces then rot in pryſon, by this onely meanes you may get a re leaſe from him, 'tis not yet come to his Vncles hearing, ſend ſpeedily for the creditors, by this time hee's diſperate, hee'le ſet his hand to any thing, take order for his debts, or diſcharge e'm quite, a pax on him, lets be rid of a raskall. Ime yet like thoſe, whoſe riches lie in dreames, If I be wakte the're falſe, ſuch is my fate, Who ventures deeper then the deſperate ſtate. Though I haue find yet could I become new, For where I once vow, I am euer true. Out you penurious ſlaue. Ide faine knowe that. Shame. Doubt nothing, theres a Releaſe a drawing and all to which you muſt ſet your hand. But mee thinkes ifaith you might haue made ſome ſhift to diſcharge this your ſelfe, hauing in the morgage, and ne uer haue burdned my conſcience with it. Pleaſe you Madam a while to taſt the ayre in the garden? Oh heauen, I am betrayde, I know that face. Alaſſe you know at firſt ſir, I told you I had nothing: Lo, Gentlemen, before you all. In true reclaymed forme I fall, Hence-forth for euer I defie, The Glances of a ſinnefull eye, Wauing of Fans, which ſome ſuppoſe, Tricks of Fancy, Treading of Toes, Wringing of Fingers, byting the Lip, The wanton gate th' alluring Trip, All ſecret friends and priuate meetings, Cloſe borne letters, and Baudes greetings, Fayning excuſe to weomens Labours, When we are ſent for to'th next Neighbours, Taking falſe Phiſicke, and nere ſtart, To be let blood, tho ſigne be at heart, Remouing chambers, ſhifting beds, To welcome Frends in husbands ſteads, Them to enioy, and you to marry, They firſt ſerud, while you muſt tarry, They to ſpend and you to gather, They to get and you to father, Theſe and thouſand thouſand more, New reclaymed I now abhore.
Maſſe that's true, the Ieſt will bee of ſome continu ance, let mee ſee, Horſes now, a bottes on em; Stay, I haue acquaintance with a madde Hoſte, neuer yet Bawde to thee, I haue rinzde the whoreſons gums in Mull-ſack many a time and often, put but a good Tale into his eare now, ſo it come off cleanely, and there's Horſe and man for vs I dare war rant thee. Why then all's furniſht; I ſhall goe nigh to catch that olde Foxe mine Vncle, tho hee make but ſome amends for my vndooing, yet there's ſome comfort in't — hee cannot other wiſe chooſe (tho it bee but in hope to coozen mee agen) but ſupply any haſtie want that I bring to towne with mee, the De uice well and cunningly carryed, the name of a riche Widdow, and foure hundred a yeare in good earth, will ſo coniure vp a kinde of Vſurers loue in him to mee, that hee will not onely deſire my preſence, which at firſt ſhall ſcarce bee granted him, Ile keepe off a purpoſe, but I ſhall finde him ſo officious to de ſerue, ſo ready to ſupply, I know the ſtate of an old mans af fection ſo well, if his Nephew bee poore indeed, why hee letts God alone with him, but if hee be once rich, then heele bee the firſt man that helpes him. I owe thee for that Ieſt, bee gone, here's all my wealth; prepare thy ſelfe, away? Ile to mine Hoſte withall poſſible haſt, and with the beſt Art, & moſt profitable forme, powre the ſweet circumſtance into his eare, which ſhall haue the gift to turne all the waxe to hunny; how no; oh the right worſhipful Seniors of our Country — What Geldings are in the houſe of thine owne? anſwer me to that firſt. Marke mee what I ſay, Ile tell thee ſuch a tale in thine eare, that thou ſhalt truſt mee ſpite of thy teeth, furniſh me with ſome money, wille, nille, and ride vp with mee thy ſelfe Contra voluntatem et profeſſion em. Now ſir, the caſe ſtands thus, good mine Hoſt, if thou lou'ſt my happineſſe aſſiſt me. Nay thats not all neither, prethee take truce with thy ioy, and liſten to mee, thou know'ſt I haue a wealthy Vncle i'th Citty, ſome-what the wealthier by my follyes; the report of this fortune well and cunningly carried, might be a meanes to drawe ſome goodneſſe from the Vſuring Raſcall, for I haue put her in hope already of ſome eſtate that I haue eyther in land or money: now if I be found true in neither, what may I expect but a ſuddaine breach of our loue, vtter diſſolution of the match, and confuſion of my fortunes for euer. With thee? why will I deſire to thriue in my purpoſe? will I hugge foure hundred a yeare? I that know the miſery of nothing? will that man wiſh a riche widdow, that has nere a hole to put his head in? with thee mine Hoſte, why beleeue it, ſooner with thee then with a Couy of Counſellors? Hard at Parke-end. Why there wee let off together, keepe full time, my thoughts were ſtriking then iuſt the ſame number. Our merry nights—which nere ſhall bee more ſeene. Haſt thou the writings? Prethee ſtay, and behold two the moſt prodigious raſ cals that euer ſlipt into the ſhape of men, Dampit ſirrah, and young Gulfe, his fellow Cater-piller. Heard of him? why man he that ha's loſt both his eares, may heare of him, a famous infamous Trampler of time; his owne phraze: note him well, that Dampit ſirrah, hee in the vn euen Beard, and the Serge cloake, is the moſt notorious, vſu ring, blaſphemous, Atheiſticall, Brothell, vomiting raſcall, that wee haue in theſe latter times now extant, whoſe firſt begin ning was the ſtealing of a maſtie Dogge from a Farmers houſe. True, the next Towne he came at, hee ſet the Dogs to gether by'th eares. Holla. A plot, a plot: to Boate ſhee's ſtole away. Follow, enquire, old Hoord my Vncles Aduerſary— Thrice miſerable wretch. What would you with me now, my Vncles ſpitefull aduerſary.
Whoſe that; I wonder how hee breathes, ha's conſum'd all vpon that Curtizan? Faith about a purchaſe, fetching ouer a yong heire; Maiſter Hoord my brother hauing waſted much time in beating the bargayne, what did me old Lucre ▪ but as his conſcience mou'd him, knowing the poore Gentleman ▪ ſtept in betweene e'm and couzned him himſelfe. This was e'en it ſir, yet for all this I know no reaſon but the match might go forward betwixt his wiues Sonne and my Neece, what tho there bee a diſſention betweene the two olde men, I ſee no reaſon it ſhould put a difference betweene the two yonger, tis as naturall for old folkes to fall out, as for yong to fall in? A ſcholler comes a wooing to my Neece, well, hee's wiſe, but he's poore, her Sonne comes a wooing to my Neece, well, hees a foole, but hees rich — Pray now is not a rich foole better then a poore Philo ſopher. She now remaines at London with my brother her ſecond Vncle, to learne faſhions, practiſe Muſicke, the voyce betweene her lips, and the violl betweene her legges, ſhee'le bee fitt for a conſort very ſpeedily, a thouſand good pound is her portion, if ſhe marry, weele ride vp and be merry,— I am glad of this newes. I promiſe you Maiſter Cock-pit ſhe's a mighty rich widdow. Who widdow Medler, ſhee lies open to much rumour. Nay tak't of my word if you beleeue that, you beleeue the leaſt. Oh ſir there's policy in that to preuent better ſuiters. He little dreames of our comming, heele wonder to ſee his creditors vpon him. Maiſter Wit-good I haue forborne my money long. He ſaies true yfaith. I, if we could be content a ſhame take vs. No, good Maiſter Wit-good, Would twere as much as we dare truſt you with? Do you heare ſir, I may deſerue your cuſtome heereafter, pray let my money be accepted before a ſtrangers, here's fortie pound I receiu'd as I came to you, if that may ſtand you in any ſtead make vſe on't, nay pray ſir, tis at your ſeruice — Let none of them ſee it I beſeech you. I hope I ſhall be firſt in your remembrance after the mar riage rites. So, what do you walke ſirs? Wee doo ſir. The better firſt to worke you to beleife, Know neither of vs owe him flattery, Nor tother malice, but vnbribed cenſure, So helpe vs our beſt fortunes. That Wit-good is a riotous vndon man, Imperfect both in fame and in eſtate: His debts welthier then he, and executions In waite for his due body, we'ele maintayne With our beſt credit, and our deereſt bloud. What we ſpeake, Our liues and meanes are ready to make good. Nay beleeue it widdow, You had not onely matcht your ſelfe to wants, But in an euill and vnnaturall ſtocke. Then with a new and pure affection, Behold you Gentleman, graue, kinde and rich: A match worthy your ſelfe, eſteeming him, You do regard your ſtate. Hee can ioyne land to land, and will poſſeſſe you of what you can deſire. There tis deceitfull, Where flattery, want, and imperfection lies: But none of theſe in him? puſh — Come you widdowes are euer moſt back-ward, when you ſhould doe your ſelues moſt good, but were it to marry a chin not worth a haire now, then you would bee forward ynough? come, clap hands, a match. Twas well deuized. We're engade ſir. Tis for our credits now to ſee't well ended. Did not I vſe moſt art to win the widdow. I was the firſt that mou'd her. Come you roomes fitteſt: The widdow gon? No more good ſir, it is a wrong to vs, To ſee you iniur'd in a cauſe ſo iuſt: Weele ſpend our liues, but we will right our friends, Ioyne hearts, ioyne hands, In wedlocks bands, Neuer to part, till death cleaue your heart, You ſhall forſake all other women, You Lords, Knights, Gentlemen, and Yeomen. What my tongue ſlips, make vp with your lips. Weele pawne our credits widdow, what he ſpeakes ſhall be performde in fullneſſe. Weele do our beſt ſir?—ſee where he comes, E'en ioyleſſe and regardleſſe of all forme. Come fie? That vengeance is your Vncles, being done More in deſpite to him, then wrong to you, But we bring comfort now,— Berlady and thats no toye ſir: Now you may certifye the widdow? Withall our hearts, and wee ſhall ioye to ſee your enimy ſo mockt: Ile wayte theſe 7. howers but Ile ſee him caught, A my Troth ſhees the wiſer, ſhe has made the happier choyſe, and I wonder of what Stuffe thoſe widdowes hearts are made of, that wil marry vnfledgd Boies, before comely thrumb chind Gentlemen. What boye? So, ſo, ſo, ſo, it warmes me at the heart, I loue a life to ſee Dogs vpon men; oh here hee comes. Oh wee may ſpeake with you now ſir, whats become of your rich widdow, I thinke you may caſt your cap at the wid dow, may you not ſir. Come, come ſir, what ſay you extempore now to your bill of a hundred pound: a ſweet debt, for froating your doublets. No ſir, wel'e keepe you out of breath ſtill, then we ſhall be ſure you will not run away from vs. Do you talke of Reaſonable time to vs? Thats our deſires ſir. Sir. Come hether Maiſter Wit-good come hether, be rulde by fooles once: Take hold of his offer pax on her, let her goe, if your debts were once diſcharg'd, I would helpe you to a widdow my ſelfe worth ten of her. Cuds mee, as pat as can be, there's a widdow left for you, ten thouſand in mony, beſide Plate, Iewells et caetera I warrant it a match, wee can do all in all with her, prethee diſpatch weele carry thee to her preſently. With much a doe ſir, we haue got him to conſent. Some eight ſcore od pounds ſir. You muſt make it a marke ſir,— Tis ſomthing wanting ſir, yet it ſhall be ſufficient. Why do you thinke we were in earneſt yfaith? carry you to a rich widdow, wee ſhould get much credit by that; a noted Rioter a contemptible prodigall, twas a Trick we haue amongſt vs, to get in our mony, fare you well ſir.
Oh the common Rioter, take no note of him. We haue heard ſo much. What was the quarrell ſir? And was this all ſir: I marry ſir? One would think ſo yfaith? So are we by my faith. Why haue you euer heard of her. And to ſee how cloſſe hee keepes it. We heare you are to be married ſuddainely to a rich Coun try widdow? Sweete Gentleman? Faith wee heard you brought vp a rich widdow ſir, and were ſuddainely to marry her. I goe—take no care ſir for money to furniſh you, within this houre ile ſend you ſufficient: come Maiſter Cock-pit wee both ſtay for you. But Maiſter Hoord, are you ſure he is not ith houſe now? And for his Vncle.— Come widdow come. You ſhall pardon mee for that ſir, Maiſter Hoord knowes I tooke her at beſt vantage. He will needs beare me downe that his art onely, wrought with the widdow moſt. But it was I that tooke her at the bound. Why how Maiſter Wit-good, fie, you a firme ſcholler, and an vnderſtanding Gentleman, and giue your beſt partes to paſſion. Cheere thy ſelfe man, there's hope of her ifayth? Faith ſo will I. He a rich widdow? who a prodigall, a dayly Rioter, and a nightly vomiter, he a widow of account? he a hole ith counter. Here's mine of forty, You ſhall pardon vs for that ſir, we know you haue too faire a tong of your owne, you ouer-came vs to lately, a ſhame take you, we are like to looſe all that for want of witneſſes, wee dealt in policy then, alwaies when we ſtriue to bee moſt politi que we proue moſt cocſkcombs, Non plus vltra. I perceiue by vs, were not ordaynde to thriue by wiſdome, and therefore wee muſt be content to be Tradeſ-men. Wee muſt haue either mony or carcaſſe. We are Cittizens and know what belong toote. Harke, ile tell thee a Trick for that, I haue ſpent fiue hun dred pound in ſuites in my time, I ſhould be wiſe, thou it now a priſoner, make a releaſe, takte of my worde, whatſoeuer a man makes as long as he is in durance, tis nothing in lawe, not thus much.
You will not ſee me now, the comfort is ere it be long you will ſcarce ſee your ſelues.
speeches.1: You have heard all truth, his Vncle and my Brother, haue beene theſe three yeares mortall Aduerſaries. Two old tough ſpirits, they ſeldome meete but fight, or quarrell when tis calmeſt; I thinke their anger bee the very fire That keepes their age aliue:
A match, if it be a match? Yong Wit-good will be a gallant agen now. Foure hundred a yeare they ſay in very good land. Hee owes me a hundred pound, and I proteſt I neere lookte for a pennie. It cannot indeed? I ha loſt a ring ifaith, ile followe you preſently—but you ſhall finde it ſir, I know your youth and expences haue diſfur niſht you of all Iewells, ther's a Ruby of twenty pound price ſir, beſtowe it vpon your widdow, —what man, twill call vp her bloud to you, beſide if I might ſo much worke with you, I would not haue you beholding to thoſe bloud-ſuckers for any money. The'ar a brace of cut-throates? Send a note of all your wants to my ſhoppe and ile ſup ly you inſtantly. Shall I carry it away from e'm both then. Troth then I thanke you ſir. I boaſted leaſt, but twas I ioynd their hands, Hang him prodigall, he's ſtript of the Widdow. Here's mine of fifty. Oh tis a Secret delight we haue amongſt vs, we that are vſde to keepe birds in cages, haue the heart to keepe men in priſon, I warrant you. Maſſe partner and now you remember mee on't, there's Maiſter Muligrubs ſiſter newly falne a widdow. I haue payde for't I know't. Why wel ſayde:
Young maiſter Wit-good. Why what's the newes Bully-Hadland? Why man, why? How: let me ſee this trick, and Ile ſay thou haſt more Arte then a Coniurer. Do I loue Sack and Ginger? Come forfeitures to a Vſurer, fees to an officer, punkes to an Hoſte, and Pigs to a Parſon deſiredly? why then la. Wilt thou command me now? I am thy ſpirit, coniure me into any ſhape. No 'tis a toung with a great T my boye that winnes a widdow. Command all my beaſts ith houſe. Wilt thou but truſt the managing of thy buſineſſe with me? Thanke you for your good report yfaith ſir, and if I ſtand you not inſteed, why then let an Hoſte come off Hic & haec hoſtis, a deadly enemie to Dice, Drinke, and Venery; come where's this widdow? Feare you nothing ſir, I haue lodgd her in a houſe of credit I warrant you. Firme ſir Dampit ? ſure I haue heard of that Dampit. Hee lookt as if hee would obay the commandement well, when he began firſt with ſtealing. How the deuill came he by it? Bleſſe your venerable worſhip. Hee calles me theefe at firſt ſight, yet he little thinkes I am an Hoſt? Faith ſir, I am ſent from my Miſtriſſe to any ſufficient Gentleman indeed, to aske aduiſe vpon a doubtfull point, 'tis indifferent ſir, to whome I come, for I know none, nor did my Miſtres direct mee to any perticuler man, for ſhee's as meere a ſtranger here as my ſelfe, onely I found your worſhip within, and tis a thing I euer lou'd ſir to be diſpacht as ſoone as I can: Fayth a Cuntry Gentlewoman and a widdow ſir, yeſter day was the firſt flight of vs, but now ſhee entends to ſtay till a little Tearme buſineſſe be ended. It runnes there in the writings ſir, among her Lands, widdow Medler? Yes, I wa •• nt you, haue you ſir, not the rich widdowe in Staffordſheere : No doubt your worſhip might do much then, but ſhe's fayrely promiſt to a bachiler already. A Country Gentleman too, one whome your worſhip knowes not Ime ſure: has ſpent ſome fewe follies in his youth, but marriage by my fayth begins to call him home, my Miſtris loues him ſir, and loue couers faults you know, one maiſter VVit-good if euer you haue heard of the Gentleman: Thats his name indeede ſir; my Miſtris is like to bring him to a goodly ſeate yonder, foure hundred a yeare by my faith, I ſir ▪ A Leſterſhire gentleman ſir. Fayth he brought her vp to towne ſir, has the beſt card in all the bunch fort, her heart: and I know my Miſtris will bee married, ere ſhe goe downe, nay Ile ſweare that, for ſhe's none of thoſe widdowes that will goe downe firſt, and bee married af ter, ſhe hates that I can tell you ſir. Why do's your worſhip know him ſir? Then your worſhippe may ſaue mee a labour, for I had charge giuen me to enquire after him. No doubt ſir: Why very true ſir. Since your worſhippe has ſo much knowledge in him, can you reſolue me Sir what his liuing might bee, my duty bindes me ſir to haue a care of my miſtris eſtate, ſhe has beene euer a good miſtris to me though I ſay it, many welthy Sui ters has ſhee Nonſuted for his ſake, yet tho her Loue bee ſo fixt, a man cannot tell whether his Non-performance may helpe to remoue it ſir; hee makes vs beleeue hee has lands and liuing. Nay I know not ifaith. Is he ſo ſir, to ſee how rumor will alter, truſt me ſir we heard once he had no lands, but all lay morgagde to an Vncle he has in towne here. I can aſſure you ſir twas credibly reported to my Miſtris. That was my ſaying ſtill ſir. I do beſeech your ſir do me the fauour to conceale it, what a Beaſt was I to vtter ſo much: pray ſir doe mee the kindneſſe to keepe it in, I ſhall haue my coate pull'd ore my eares, ant ſhould bee knowne, for the truth is an't pleaſe your worſhippe, to preuent much rumour and many ſuiters, they entend to bee married verie ſuddenly and priuately. So I might haue no anger ſir— I dare truſt your worſhip ſir, but I'me a ſtranger to your houſe, and to auoyde al Intelligencers I deſire your worſhippes eare. Pleaſe you ſir now I haue begunne with your worſhip when ſhall I attend, for your aduice vpon that doubtfull poynt, I muſt come warily now. The time ſhall cauſe my attendance. I am the worſt of ſixe ſir, good inough for blew-coates. Not ſo ſir. Maiſter Wit-good your Vncle— A prety familiar Priggin raſkall, hee has his part with out booke? What Miſtres? The deuill of ring I can finde? My Miſtris? is ſhe not here ſir? Shee ſent me for a Ring. What? I trac'de e'm neerely.— And heare for certaine, they haue tooke Cole-harbor. My life for yours ſir now, I know my Miſtriſſes minde to well toward your Nephew, let things be in preparation, and ile traine her hether in moſt excellent faſhion: Maiſter Wit-good. A thing that concernes my Miſtris ſir. I and you knaue too, (cry your worſhippe mercy) you are both like to come into trouble I promiſe you ſir, a praecon tract I feare they haue too much proofe on't ſir, old Lucre he runs mad vp and downe and will to lawe as faſt as he can, yong Wit-good layde hold on by his creditors, hee exclaymes vpon you a tother ſide, ſaies you haue wrought his vndoing, by the in iurious detayning of his contract. He will haue vtmoſt ſatiſfaction. The lawe ſhall giue him recompence he ſaies. True ſir— A prety ſhift yfaith, I commend a woman when ſhee can make away a letter from her huſband handſomely, and this was cleanely done by my troth. This will be ſome reuenge yet. Yes ſir, there are as good Teirs in the houſe, as any are in England. Has ſhe ſo, the better for her ▪ and the worſe for you.
speeches.Wit,: I haue beene laying all the Towne for thee.
speeches.Wit: Will the report of a Widdow of foure hundred a yeare boye, make thee leape, and ſing, and dance, and come to thy place agen. I am ſory you take it in that ſence ſir. My life.
Ile be her Seruing-man for once. I knew't, ſhall we then ſee our merry dayes agen? A ſigne he ſhould follow the law by my faith. Yet that report goes currant. Is your worſhip his Vncle ſir. That's none of my name ſir.
Nay good Maiſter Lucre, and you Maiſter Hoord ▪ anger is the winde which you ▪ re both too much troubled with all. Nay ſweet Maiſter Lucre.
Shall my aduerſary thus dayly afront mee, ripping vp the old wound of our malice, which three Summers could not cloſe vp, into which wound the very ſight of him, drops ſcald ing Lead inſteed of Balſamum. Was it the part of a friend: no, rather of a Iew, marke what I ſay, when I had beaten the buſh to the laſt bird, or as I may terme it, the price to a pound, then like a cunning Vſurer to come in the euening of the bargaine, and gleane all my hopes in a minute, to enter as it were at the back-doore of the purchaſe, for thou nere camſt the right way by it. Thou that canſt defeate thy owne Nephew, Lucre, lap his lands into bonds, and take the extremity of thy kindreds forfeitures becauſe hee's a rioter, a waſt-thrift, a brothell-mai ſter, and ſo forth— what may a Stranger expect from thee, but Ʋ ulnera delacerata, as the Poet ſayes, delacerate dealing? What's all to thee? nothing, nothing; ſuch is the gulfe of thy deſire, and the Wolfe of thy conſcience, but be aſ ſured old pecunious lucre, if euer fortune ſo bleſſe me, that I may be at leiſure to vexe thee, or any meanes ſo fauour me, that I may haue oportunitie to mad thee, I will purſue it with that flame of hate, that ſpirit of malice, vnrepreſſed wrath, that I will blaſt thy comforts. I will ſo croſſe thee, So without mercy fret thee. Dooſt ſcoffe at my iuſt anger? oh that I had as much power as vſury ha's ouer thee? Toade! Serpent.
Why Hoord, Hoord, Hoord, Hoord, Hoord ; may I not paſſe in the ſtate of quietneſſe to mine owne houſe, anſwer mee to that ▪ before witneſſe, and why? What ſay I Maiſter Dampit ? I ſay nothing but that you are very weake, Why Maiſter Dampit I neuer deceiu ▪ d you in al my life? I care not what you ſay Maiſter Dampit ? Fie Maiſter Dampit, a Gentleman and haue ſuch words. No, maiſter Dampit, and there's a Gentleman comes a wooing to me, and he doubts nothing but that you will get mee from him: Come will you riſe and goe to bed ſir? They be the ſtincking nailes of his trampling feete, and he talkes of burning of hornes: Ha, ha, ha. Why Maiſter Dampit if you hold on as you begin, and lie a little longer, you neede not take care how to diſpoſe your wealth, you'le make the Vintner your heire. Good words Maiſter Dampit, to ſpeake before a maide and a virgin. Sweete tearmes, my Miſtris ſhall know e'm. Pray Gentlemen depart, his howers come vpon him, ſleepe in my boſome, ſleepe.
speeches.Dam :: I, if I would either haue thee or lie with thee for two thouſand pound, would I might bee dambd, why thou baſe im pudent queane of foolery, flattery, and cockſcombry, are you an ſwerd? She's as fine a Philoſipher of a ſtinkards wife, as any within the liberties,—fah, fah Audry: Foh, I thinke they burne hornes in Barnards Inne, if e uer I ſmelt ſuch an abhominable ſtinck, vſury forſake me:
speeches.Aud :: Fooh— How now Maiſter Dampit ? It waites for you aboue ſir?
speeches.Hoor,: Vpon my life, my aduerſary, Gentlemen.
speeches.Hoor: Ha, ha, ha. Sayſt ſo? ſend e'm all in!—to ſee ten men ride after mee in watchet liueries with Orenge-tawny capes, twill cut his combe ifayth, how now? of what occupation are you ſir. From e'm all brother, and I may tell you, I had mighty enemies, thoſe that ſtuck ſore, old Lucre is a ſore foxe I can tell you brother.
speeches.Luc :: Why ſay it did, you might haue knowne my minde; I could haue ſoone reſtorde it. You muſt conceiue it a right Nephewe now, to doe you good, I am content to do this. Why Nephew ſhall I trace thee ſtill a lier? wilt make mee mad is not yon thing the widdow.
speeches.Luc:: Why and there's no time paſt, and rather then my ad uerſary ſhould thus thw'art my hopes, I would — Nay more I will eſtate him In farder bleſſings, he ſhall be my heire ▪ I haue no Sonne, Ile binde my ſelfe to that condition. He ſhall ſee all performde and bring you word. Nephew what cheere? alaſſe poore Gentleman how art thou changd? call thy freſh bloud into thy cheekes agen, ſhee comes— I ſhall haue great ioy there, when he has borne away the widdow. Probo tibi, Nephew: Hee that knowes a woman to bee a queane muſt needes bee a knaue, thou ſayſt thou knowſt her to bee one, ergo if ſhee bee a queane thou'rt a knaue:
speeches.Lu:: I do beleeue you, here's your owne honeſt ſeruant, Ile take him along wi • h me. A word Nephew? A, heres a leſſon Rioter for you.
I and his Nephew deſperate: But I thinke the deuill had no ſteele Bedſtaffes, he goes beyond him for that. Is this the ſick trampler, why he is onely bed-red with drincking. Fah, loathſome?
speeches.Lu :: Sweete Gentlemen cheere him vp, I will but fetch the morgage, and returne to you inſtantly. A good old boy,—wife Girnne? The wedding daies at hand, prethee ſweete wife, ex preſſe thy houſwifery, thou'rt a fine Cooke I knowte, thy firſt husband married thee out of an Aldermans kitchin, go too, he raiſde thee for rayſing of paſte, what, here's none but friends, moſt of our beginnings muſt bee winckt at, Gentlemen I enuite you all to my Nephewes wedding againſt Thurſday morning: He laught at me, gentlemen, ha, ha, ha: Then thou'rt a knaue:
speeches.1:: Sorrow of mee what a ſigh was there ſir, nine ſuch wid dowes are not worth it.
speeches.Hoſt: May I ſpeake one word with you in priuate ſir?
Do you call vs diuuills, you ſhall find vs Puritanes beare him away, let em talke as they go, we'le not ſtand to heare 'em, ah ſir, am I a deuile, I ſhall thinke the better of my ſelfe as long as I liue, a Deuill ifaith.
Yes ſir, there are ſome ith hall, that waite for your wor ſhips liking, and deſire to be entertainde. They are men fit for your worſhip ſir. Ther's a coach come to'th doore ſir. Your worſhips brother with an other antient Gentle man, are newly allighted Sir.
A Taylor, an't pleaſe your worſhip. Anon ſir.
A Fawlkner an't pleaſe your worſhip—
speeches.Faul:: And weele make you worſhip admire ſir:
speeches.Hoo :: Make e'm all trim fellowes, lowſe e'm well, eſpecially my huntſman, and cut all their beards of the Polonian faſhion: my perfumer: Maiſter Oneſiphorus Hoord, why now our company be gins to come in: my deere and kind brother welcome ifaith. Ha?
speeches.P • r:: It ſhall be carefully performde ſir.
speeches.Hun :: And weele ſhow you that ſir, ſhall deſerue your wor ſhippes fauour?
speeches.Hoo,: Shall I compound? A ritch widdow,—one widdow medler.
speeches.Hoo:: Go too then, tell your mony in the meane time, you ſhall finde little leſſe there,—come Maiſter Wit-good you are ſo vnwil ling to do your ſelfe good now, welcome honeſt Scriuener, now you ſhall heare the releaſe read,— Deſire your miſtris you knaue, to taſt e'm all ouer, ſhe • has better Skill. Gentlemen! Oh, nor Lands, nor liuing?
Be it known, to al men by theſe preſents, that I Theodorus Wit-good, Gentleman, ſole Nephew to Pecunious Lucre, hauing vniuſtly made title and claime, to one Iane Medler, late widdow of Anthory Medler, and now wife to Walkadine Hoord, in con ſideration of a competent ſom of mony to diſcharge my debts, do for euer hereafter diſclaime any title, right, eſtate, or intereſt in or to the ſayd widdow late in the occupation of the ſayd An thony Medler, and now in the occupation of Walkadine Hoord, as alſo neither to laye claime, by vertue of any former contract, grant, promiſe or demiſe, to any of her Mannor, Mannorhouſes, Parkes, Groues, Meadow-grounds, arrable lands, Barnes, ſtacks, Stables, Doue-holes, and Cunny-borrowes, togither with al her cattell, money, plate, iewells, borders, chaines, bracelets, furni tures, hangings, moueables, or immouerables in wittneſſe wher of I the ſayd Theodorus Wit-good, haue enterchangeably ſet to my hand and ſeale before theſe preſents, the daie, & date aboue written.
Meete me preſently, that note directs you, I would not be ſuſpected our happineſſe attends vs, farewell?
speeches.Dam:: What? ſir Triſtram? you come and ſee a weake man here, a very weake man,— Oh, I haue pray'd too much poore man. Alaſſe you come at an ill time, I cannot ſpare it ifayth, I ha but two thouſand ith houſe. Oh, my boſome ſir Lancelot, how cheere I? thy pre ſence is reſtoratiue: I am glad of that ifayth; —prethee what? There twas ifayth, nothing but the pride of the Sack and ſo certifie e'm, fetch Sack ſirrah. Hang thy virginity, vpon the pole of carnality.
speeches.Damp:: Out you gernatiue queane, the mullipood of villany, the Spinner of concupiſcency. Out you babliaminy, you vnfetherd cremitoryed queane, you culliſance of ſcabiofity. Sir Lancelot ? let me buſſe thee ſir Lancelot, thou art the onely friend that I honor and reſpect.
Yee gentlemen are you here before vs? how is hee now? I thanke you for that Maiſter Dampit. Gentlemen, and you loue mee, let mee ſtep behinde you, and one of you fall a talking of me to him. What a rogues this? Nay Gentlemen, he ſhall ſhow you more Tricks yet, ile giue you another taſt of him: His memory is vpon departing. Maſſe then twill be quite gon: before he drinke that, tell him theres a cuntry client come vp, and here attends for his Learned aduice, Pleaſe your good worſhip, I am a poore man ſir.— I would entreate your worſhips deuice in a iuſt and honeſt cauſe ſir.— I had but one houſe left me in all the world ſir which was my fathers, my Grand-fathers, my great Grandfathers, and now a Villaine has vniuſtly wrung me out, and tooke poſſeſſi on out. Alaſſe, ant pleaſe your worſhip, I haue ſmall friends and leſſe mony. I thanke your worſhip for your hot Counſell ſir.— altring but my voyce alitle, you ſee he knew me not, you may obſerue by this that a drunkards memory, holds longer in the voyce then in the perſon, but Gentlemen ſhall I ſhow you a ſight, behold the litle diue-dapper of Damnation, Gulfe the vſurer, for his time worſe then tother. Why Hoord, that maried lately the widdowe medler. faith here hee lies e'n drawing—in ſir, good canary as faſt as hee can ſir, a very weake creature truely, hee is almoſt paſt memory. This exlent, theefe rayles vpon the Theefe. 'Heele quarrell with none I warrant you, but thoſe that are bedred. Here wilbe a ſweet fraie anon, Ile leaue you gentlemen.
speeches.Lan:: Wee ſhall haue the better ſport with him, peace, and how cheeres Maiſter Dampit now? But I heare a great complaint of you Maiſter Dampit, among gallants. They ſay you are waxte proud alate, and if a friend viſit you in the after-noone, you'le ſcarce know him. Thinke you ſo ſir? Sfoote I can no longer endure the rogue, Maiſter Dampit, I come to take my leaue once agen ſir?
speeches.Lam :: Note but the miſery of this vſuring ſlaue, here hee lies like a noyſome dunghill, full of the poyſon of his druncken blaſphemies, and they to whome he bequeathes all, grudge him the very meate that feedes him, the very pillow that eaſes him, here may a vſurer behold his end, what profits it to be a ſlaue in this world, and a deuil ith next.
Who ſir Lancelot. Pythagoricall? I wonder you can raile at him ſir, he comes in loue to ſee you. Compoſde of wrongs and ſlauiſh flatteries. I'ſt poſſible? Inough. Maiſter Dampit. Tis comming forward ſir,—heres a countryman a cli ent of yours, waytes for your deepe and profound aduice ſir. You muſt draw nere ſir. What's he comes with him? Oh, I cry you mercy ſir. Nay you muſt exercize patience Maiſter Gulfe, alwayes in a ſick-mans Chamber. Nay wel'e a long with you, Maiſter Gulfe. They were indeed ſir, you ſee bould gueſtes ſir, ſoone intreated So we bachilers thinke that are not troubled with them
What? hung a liue in chaynes O Spectacle, bed ſtaffs of ſteele, O monſtrum, horrendum, Informe, Ingens cui Lumen ademptum, O Dampit, Dampit, heres a Iuſt iudgment, ſhowne vpon vſury, extortion, and trampling Villany. Is this the end of cut throate Vſury, Brothell, and blaſphemy? now maiſt thou ſee what Race a Vſu rer runnes. Ant twere not for ſhame.— Hang him vſuring raskall. A litle thing would make me beat him, now he's aſleep.
speeches.Lan,: Puſh, ſet your Strenght to his, your wit to his.
speeches.Lan :: Nay we haue inough of him ifaith, keepe him for the houſe.—Now ▪ make your beſt. For thrice his wealth, I would not haue his breſt.
speeches.Lan: Maſſe then twilbe a pittifull day when he wakes. I would be loath to ſee that day, come.
You are pleaſd to make the worſt ſir. Is this your Bride. Twill pleaſe vs well.
speeches.Ony :: You ſee we are men at an hower brother.
We hope you lack gueſſe ſir?
Ah ſirrah brother, haue you catcht vp widdow Medler. Nay Brother, harke you, come y'are diſpoſde to be mer rie? That's another matter, I was nere ſo fread in my life but that you had beene in earneſt. Liuing? Brother?
Where is ſhe, ile go ſeeke her out, I long to haue a ſmack at her lips. You ſayd ſhe was your wife? By your troth Brother? Troth I am not well of a ſuddaine? I muſt craue pardon brother, I came to ſee you, but I cannot ſtay dinner yfaith.
By your leaue Maiſter Hoord. In your old age doate on a Curtizan— Nay Maſter Hoord:
speeches.Lim,: But you haue ſhowne your folly too much here.
Fie, fie, a man of your repute and name, Youle feaſt your friends but cloye e'm firſt with ſhame.
speeches.Wit:: Why la, you are ſo hard a beleefe Vncle, by my troth ſhe's a whore. Negatur Argumentum Vncle.
